title: Mind only
hookLine: the Yogacara school: how the mind shapes the world it sees

lines: WHAT IF WAKING IS SHAPED TOO?
cards: A dream can hold a street, a house, a stranger who speaks, even a fear that makes the heart race. While it lasts, all of it seems solid and outside. Then you wake, and it was all made by the mind.
Vasubandhu, the brother who changed his mind, builds one of his short verse works around exactly this kind of example. He asks: what if waking life is shaped by the mind far more than it seems?

teach.b: Tradition explains Yogacara as the practice of yoga, the path of meditators. The school grew from the teachings tradition credits to Asanga and Maitreya, and from Vasubandhu's verses. Its other name is mind only.
In his Twenty Verses, Vasubandhu argues that, as in a dream, places and times and other beings can appear vividly with nothing outside the mind behind them. Then a stranger picture.

teach.h: A RIVER OF WATER, A RIVER OF PUS.
teach.b: Where people see a river of water, he says, hungry ghosts see a river of pus. Same river, different minds, different worlds.

Yogacara teachers also describe a deep layer of mind, the storehouse consciousness, where every action leaves a seed. When a seed ripens, it shapes how the next moment looks. So yesterday's anger tints what you see today.

teach.h: NO WORLD, OR NO RAW WORLD?
teach.b: Some readers, in India, Tibet and today, take Yogacara to say there's no world outside the mind at all.
Others say it describes experience: we never meet the world raw, only as our minds have shaped it, and that's what practice works on.
Madhyamaka teachers in Tibet debated Yogacara closely, and Tibetan monastic colleges still study both schools.
A much older line, from the Dhammapada in Max Müller's translation, points in a similar direction: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Yogacara takes that thought its own way.
The mind doesn't just react to the world. It colors it.

how: Yogacara texts are studied in Tibetan monastic curricula and in East Asian Buddhism, where the Faxiang school carried them, and their account of mind and seeds shapes how teachers in those traditions explain meditation.

games.q: you and a hungry ghost stand at the same river. you see water. what does the ghost see, in Vasubandhu's picture?
games.why: same river, different minds, different worlds. Vasubandhu uses it to show how the mind shapes what it meets.

practice: Pick something in front of you, or a person you'll see later, and notice the color your mind already gives it: pleasant, annoying, boring, dear. Ask where that color came from, a memory, a mood, a habit.
You don't have to remove it; just see it as a color laid on top, and look at the thing underneath for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Yogacara. The path of meditators, also called mind only: the school of Asanga and Vasubandhu that looks at how the mind shapes the world it sees. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit Yogacara: yoga, practice, and acara, conduct: the path of the meditators.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind colors it. Same river, different minds, and so different worlds. Rest well.
